details:
**"The Charge of the Light Brigade"**
Tennyson's most famous poem, about a doomed British cavalry charge at the Battle of Balaclava (1854) during the Crimean War. It opens "Half a league, half a league, / Half a league onward," describes "cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them," and notes "Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die." Its six stanzas all end with "six hundred," as "Into the valley of Death / Rode the six hundred," and it asks "When can their glory fade?" since "All the world wondered."

**In Memoriam A.H.H.**
A long elegy for Tennyson's close friend Arthur Henry Hallam, who died suddenly in 1833 at age 22, written over seventeen years. It contains the famous lines "'Tis better to have loved and lost / Than never to have loved at all."

**"Nature, red in tooth and claw"**
A phrase from In Memoriam expressing doubt about a loving God in the face of a violent natural world. The poem also says "we have but faith: we cannot know," prays "Thou wilt not leave us in the dust," and includes the section "Ring out, wild bells," supposedly inspired by the bells of Waltham Abbey Church.

**"Ulysses"**
A dramatic monologue in which an aged Ulysses (Odysseus), an "idle king" back on Ithaca, decides to set sail again. He leaves his "sceptre and the isle" to his "blameless" son Telemachus, calls himself "a part of all that I have met," vows to "drink life to the lees," "follow knowledge like a sinking star," "sail beyond the sunset," and perhaps "touch the Happy Isles." It ends "Tho' much is taken, much abides... To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield."

**"Crossing the Bar"**
A short late poem that uses a ship crossing the sandbar out to sea as a metaphor for death. It begins "Sunset and evening star, / And one clear call for me!", includes "Twilight and evening bell, / And after that the dark!" and ends hoping "to see my Pilot face to face / When I have crost the bar." Tennyson asked that it be placed at the end of all editions of his poems.

**"The Lady of Shalott"**
A poem about a cursed woman in a tower on an island near Camelot who may only see the world through a mirror while weaving. It begins "On either side the river lie / Long fields of barley and of rye," and the fifth line of each nine-line stanza ends in "Camelot." When she looks directly at Sir Lancelot, "The mirror crack'd from side to side," and she floats down the river toward Camelot, dying while singing her last song.

**"Tithonus"**
A dramatic monologue by the mythical Tithonus, who was granted immortality but not eternal youth and now longs to die. It begins "The woods decay, the woods decay and fall," and its fourth line, "And after many a summer dies the swan," gave Aldous Huxley the title After Many a Summer Dies the Swan.

**"The Lotos-Eaters"**
A poem based on the episode in The Odyssey where Odysseus's men eat the lotus and lose all desire to return home. Its "Choric Song" begins "There is sweet music here that softer falls / Than petals from blown roses on the grass," and the mariners sing "Hateful is the dark-blue sky, / Vaulted o'er the dark-blue sea."

**"Break, Break, Break"**
A short elegy, also written for Arthur Hallam, addressed to the sea: "Break, break, break, / On thy cold gray stones, O Sea!" The speaker envies "the fisherman's boy" and "the sailor lad," and mourns that "the tender grace of a day that is dead / Will never come back to me."

**Idylls of the King**
A cycle of twelve narrative poems retelling the legend of King Arthur, based largely on Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur. Its episodes include "Gareth and Lynette."

**"Mariana"**
A poem inspired by Shakespeare's Measure for Measure, about Mariana, who waits in her "moated grange" for Angelo, the lover who abandoned her. Each stanza ends with a refrain like "My life is dreary, / He cometh not," she said; / She said, "I am aweary, aweary, / I would that I were dead!"

**"Tears, Idle Tears" and The Princess**
"Tears, Idle Tears" is a lyric song from Tennyson's long narrative poem The Princess. It describes tears that rise "from the depth of some divine despair" when thinking of "the days that are no more."

**"The Kraken"**
A short early poem about the mythical sea monster, who "sleepeth" far "below the thunders of the upper deep." It predicts that the Kraken will rise to the surface only at the end of the world and die.

**"Locksley Hall"**
A dramatic monologue that begins "Comrades, leave me here a little, while as yet 'tis early morn," spoken by a young soldier who returns to the hall where his cousin Amy rejected him. Tennyson published a sequel decades later, "Locksley Hall Sixty Years After."

**Poet Laureate and The Foresters**
Tennyson succeeded William Wordsworth as Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom in 1850 and was later made a baron, hence "Lord Tennyson." He also wrote verse plays, including The Foresters, a play about Robin Hood with incidental music by Arthur Sullivan.
